match.reason: The bank point only defines aims, hypotheses, models and theories, while the new point teaches how data supports or refutes a claim and how error and uncertainty limit that conclusion, which is a different idea.

draft.title: Evidence for and against a hypothesis
card: A hypothesis is a testable prediction. Data that match the prediction support it. Data that clearly do not match it count as evidence against it, and may refute it.
Support is not proof. New data in the future could still disagree, so a hypothesis, model or theory is judged by how well the evidence fits it.
a mistake or flaw in method, such as a faulty instrument or a poorly controlled variable. It can push results away from the true value.
the natural doubt in any measurement, such as the limits of a ruler or variation between samples. A small sample or a large spread makes conclusions less certain.
draft.remember: Data can back or challenge an idea, but errors and uncertainty limit how strongly.

a.q: A study's data do not match a hypothesis's prediction, and the method was well controlled. What does this mean for the hypothesis?
opts: It has evidence against it and may be refuted
It has been proven true by the study
It must be kept, because the data are wrong
It cannot be tested at all
a.why: Data that clearly disagree with a prediction count as evidence against the hypothesis. Keeping it because the data are wrong is tempting, but the method was well controlled, so there is no reason to dismiss the data.
a.clue: Does the data match the prediction?

b.q: Tom predicts that a fertiliser increases the mass of tomato plants. He tests it on only three plants, and they do grow heavier, but the masses vary a lot. What can he fairly conclude?
opts: The data support the idea, but the conclusion is uncertain
The data prove the fertiliser works on all tomato plants
The data refute the hypothesis, because masses vary
The data are useless, because any result is an error
b.why: The heavier plants match the prediction, so they support it. With only three plants and a large spread, the uncertainty is high, so the support is weak and not proof. Variation alone does not refute a hypothesis.
b.clue: Think about how few plants he tested.

a.best: It has evidence against it and may be refuted

b.best: The data support the idea, but the conclusion is uncertain

problems.detail: Error is defined as 'a mistake or flaw in method'. VCE Biology treats mistakes (personal errors) as separate from systematic and random errors, and they are not counted in error analysis. A poorly controlled variable is also a validity issue rather than a measurement error. This definition clashes with the study design's terms.

Calling a hypothesis 'a testable prediction' runs it together with the prediction. The VCE study design treats a hypothesis as a tentative, testable explanation from which a prediction is made. The card then says data 'match the prediction', which mixes the two ideas.
The plants 'grow heavier', but no comparison or control group is mentioned. A careful student could argue that, without one, nothing can be concluded about the fertiliser.
The right option is the only hedged one. Every other option is absolute ('refute', 'prove ... all', 'useless ... any'), so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The card's definition of error (including 'mistakes') clashes with VCE terminology, and the card blurs hypothesis with prediction. In question b, no comparison group is mentioned, and the right option stands out as the only hedged one.

proposal.title: Evidence for and against a hypothesis
card: A hypothesis is a tentative, testable explanation. From it you make a prediction of what the results should show. Results that match the prediction support the hypothesis. Results that clearly do not are evidence against it, and may refute it.
Support is not proof. New evidence could still disagree, so a hypothesis, model or theory is judged by how well all the evidence fits it.
a consistent shift in every reading in the same direction, such as a balance that always reads 2 g too high. It affects accuracy, and repeats do not remove it.
unpredictable variation between readings, such as natural differences between plants. It creates uncertainty, so a small sample or a large spread makes support weaker. More repeats reduce its effect.
proposal.remember: Results can support or count against a hypothesis, but error and uncertainty limit how strongly.

a.q: A well-controlled study gives results that do not match the prediction made from a hypothesis. What does this mean for the hypothesis?
opts: It has evidence against it, and it may be refuted
It is supported, because the method was well controlled
It is unaffected, because only the prediction failed
It is proven true, because the method had no error
a.why: The prediction comes from the hypothesis, so results that clearly disagree with it count as evidence against the hypothesis. Saying it is unaffected is tempting, but a failed prediction reflects back on the explanation it came from.
a.clue: Where did the prediction come from?

b.q: Tom hypothesises that a fertiliser increases tomato plant mass. Three treated plants end up heavier on average than three untreated ones, but masses vary a lot. What do the results give?
opts: Weak support, limited mainly by random error
Weak support, limited mainly by systematic error
Strong support, because a control group was used
Evidence against it, because the masses vary widely
b.why: The treated plants were heavier, which matches the prediction, so the results support the hypothesis. With only three plants per group and a large spread, random error makes the support weak. Systematic error is tempting, but it is a consistent shift in every reading, not variation between plants.
b.clue: Is the variation consistent or unpredictable?

a.best: It has evidence against it, and it may be refuted

b.best: Weak support, limited mainly by random error
